explanation: H⁺ ions from the acid combine with OH⁻ ions from the base to form water. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved as spectator ions, so the mixture ends up as ordinary salt water. Nothing changes colour and no gas is given off, but the tube becomes noticeably warm because the reaction releases heat.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — acids, bases and salts; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (standard enthalpy of neutralisation, about −57 kJ per mole)

hazard.title: Lead compounds are poisonous
hazard.warning: Both the lead(II) nitrate solution and the yellow lead(II) iodide formed are poisonous. Lead builds up in the body over time rather than being cleared out, so even small repeated exposures matter. It must never be touched with bare hands, tasted, or washed down the sink.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Handle lead solutions with gloves and wash your hands afterwards. Collect all lead waste in the labelled heavy-metal waste container so it can be disposed of properly instead of entering the water supply.

explanation: Two solutions that were both clear produce a bright yellow solid. Pb²⁺ ions from the lead nitrate meet I⁻ ions from the potassium iodide and join together as lead(II) iodide, which is insoluble in water and so drops out as a precipitate. K⁺ and NO₃⁻ take no part and stay dissolved as spectator ions. This is often demonstrated as the golden rain experiment.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — solubility rules and double displacement reactions; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (solubility of lead(II) iodide)

explanation: Ag⁺ ions from the silver nitrate meet Cl⁻ ions from the sodium chloride and form silver chloride, which is insoluble and appears as a white curdy precipitate. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ remain in solution as spectator ions. This is the standard laboratory test for chloride ions. If the precipitate is left in sunlight it slowly darkens to grey or purple, because light breaks silver chloride down into silver metal.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for anions and solubility rules; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (solubility and photosensitivity of silver chloride)

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas is released
hazard.warning: The bubbles coming off the zinc are hydrogen, which burns very easily and forms an explosive mixture with the air. A naked flame brought near a large amount of collected hydrogen is dangerous.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames and hot surfaces away from the apparatus while gas is being given off, and work in a well ventilated room so the hydrogen can disperse.

explanation: Zinc sits above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it can push hydrogen out of the acid. Each zinc atom gives up two electrons and enters the solution as a Zn²⁺ ion, while H⁺ ions from the acid pick up those electrons and pair off as hydrogen gas. You see a steady stream of bubbles on the surface of the metal and the tube warms up. The zinc slowly gets smaller as it dissolves. The pH shown assumes the acid is fully used up, leaving a zinc chloride solution that is still mildly acidic.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — reactivity series and reactions of metals with acids; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (standard enthalpy of formation data)

explanation: No observable change. The only products that could possibly form are sodium iodide and potassium chloride, and both of those are soluble in water. Since nothing insoluble can form, no precipitate appears, no gas is given off and the mixture stays clear and colourless. All four ions simply stay dissolved and move about independently. This is still a real chemical result and worth knowing: mixing two salt solutions does not automatically produce a reaction.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — solubility rules for common salts

explanation: Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series, so it takes the sulfate for itself and pushes the copper out. Each zinc atom gives up two electrons and enters the solution as Zn²⁺; the Cu²⁺ ions take those electrons and become copper metal, which settles on the zinc as a reddish-brown coating. The blue colour fades as the copper(II) ions leave the solution, which is the clearest sign the reaction is working. The mixture warms up because the reaction gives out heat.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, the reactivity series and displacement reactions

explanation: Iron is above copper in the reactivity series, so it displaces copper from the solution. The iron dissolves as Fe²⁺ ions and the copper comes out of solution as a reddish-brown coating on the iron. Here the colour change is between two colours rather than fading to nothing: the blue of copper(II) sulfate is replaced by the pale green of iron(II) sulfate. This is the reaction behind the old trick of an iron nail turning copper-coloured in blue vitriol.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, the reactivity series and displacement reactions

explanation: Magnesium is far above copper in the reactivity series, so this displacement is the most vigorous of the three. The blue colour disappears quickly, copper settles out as a dark reddish-brown powder, and the mixture becomes noticeably hot — much hotter than with zinc or iron. The bigger the gap between two metals in the reactivity series, the more energy the displacement gives out.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, the reactivity series and displacement reactions

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas is released
hazard.warning: Magnesium reacts fast enough with acid to produce hydrogen in a hurry, and hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air. The tube also becomes hot enough to be uncomfortable to hold.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep all flames well away while the metal is fizzing, use a small piece of ribbon rather than a long strip, and work in a well ventilated room so the hydrogen disperses.

explanation: Magnesium is high in the reactivity series, so it displaces hydrogen from the acid quickly. The metal gives up two electrons to become Mg²⁺, and the H⁺ ions from the acid take those electrons and pair up as hydrogen gas. You see a fast stream of bubbles, the ribbon shrinks and disappears, and the tube gets hot. Compare this with iron, which does the same thing far more slowly, and with copper, which cannot do it at all.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with dilute acids

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas is released
hazard.warning: The bubbles coming off the iron are hydrogen, which burns very easily and forms an explosive mixture with air.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames and hot surfaces away from the apparatus while gas is being given off, and work in a well ventilated room.

explanation: Iron is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it displaces hydrogen from dilute acid — but it sits much lower than magnesium, so the bubbling is slow and steady rather than vigorous. The solution turns pale green as iron(II) chloride forms. The difference in speed between magnesium, zinc and iron in the same acid is one of the clearest ways to see the reactivity series in action.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with dilute acids

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas, and the water turns strongly alkaline
hazard.warning: Calcium releases hydrogen steadily as it reacts, and hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air. The calcium hydroxide left behind is strongly alkaline and attacks skin and eyes.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames away, add only a small granule of calcium at a time, and wear eye protection. Rinse any splashes off the skin with plenty of water.

explanation: Calcium is reactive enough to displace hydrogen from cold water, which magnesium cannot do. The granule sinks and fizzes steadily, giving off hydrogen, and the water becomes cloudy white because calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble — the little that dissolves gives the strongly alkaline solution known as limewater, and the rest stays as a white suspension. Sodium and potassium do the same thing far more violently, which is why they are demonstrated only by a teacher.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with water

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas, and the apparatus is hot
hazard.warning: This reaction needs steam, so the apparatus is at boiling point throughout, and the hydrogen given off burns very easily.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames away from where the hydrogen escapes, and let the apparatus cool before handling it. Never seal the tube — trapped steam and gas must be able to escape.

explanation: Magnesium hardly touches cold water, but it reacts readily with steam. That is why nothing happens in this vessel until it is heated to about 100 °C. Once steam is present, the magnesium is oxidised to white magnesium oxide and hydrogen is driven off. The oxide is basic, so the little that dissolves leaves the water alkaline. This contrast — nothing in cold water, a clear reaction in steam — is exactly why the reactivity series has to be read alongside the conditions.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with water and steam

explanation: No observable change. Copper sits BELOW hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot push hydrogen out of the acid — no bubbles, no dissolving, no colour change, however long you wait. This is the single most useful "nothing happens" in the whole reactivity series: it is why copper is used for water pipes and roofing while iron rusts away, and it is the dividing line the series is really about. Zinc, iron and magnesium all sit above hydrogen and all fizz in this same acid.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, position of hydrogen in the reactivity series

explanation: No observable change. Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot take the sulfate away from it — the copper stays as solid metal and the zinc stays in solution. Displacement only runs one way: a more reactive metal pushes out a less reactive one, never the other way round. Putting zinc into copper(II) sulfate gives a clear reaction; putting copper into zinc sulfate gives nothing at all.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, displacement runs only from more reactive to less reactive

explanation: No observable change. Zinc is below magnesium in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace magnesium from its salt. Compare this with zinc in copper(II) sulfate, where zinc is the more reactive metal and the reaction runs easily. Testing a metal against several different salt solutions, and noting which combinations do nothing, is exactly how the order of the reactivity series was worked out in the first place.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, establishing the order of the reactivity series

explanation: Every acid reacts with every carbonate in the same way: acid plus carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide. The carbonate ion takes two H⁺ ions from the acid to make carbonic acid, which is so unstable that it immediately falls apart into water and carbon dioxide — which is why you see fizzing rather than anything staying in solution. The gas that bubbles off turns limewater milky, and that is how you prove it is carbon dioxide.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with carbonates

explanation: Marble chips are calcium carbonate, and they fizz steadily in dilute hydrochloric acid, giving off carbon dioxide and slowly shrinking away. Because the chips are solid lumps the reaction proceeds at a rate you can watch and time, which is why this exact combination is the standard experiment for studying how surface area, concentration and temperature change the speed of a reaction. This is also the reaction that eats away limestone buildings in acid rain.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with carbonates

explanation: A hydrogencarbonate fizzes with acid just as a carbonate does, but it only needs one H⁺ per formula unit because it already carries one of its own hydrogens. The striking thing here is the temperature: the mixture gets COLDER, not hotter. Most acid–base reactions give out heat, so this is a rare and useful example of an endothermic reaction — one that takes heat in from its surroundings. That is why an instant cold pack can be made from much the same chemistry.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with hydrogencarbonates; Chemistry 9 — exothermic and endothermic changes

explanation: This is THE test for carbon dioxide. Limewater is a clear solution of calcium hydroxide; bubbling carbon dioxide through it produces calcium carbonate, which is almost insoluble, so it appears as a fine white solid that makes the clear liquid turn milky. Nothing else in ordinary school chemistry does this, which is what makes the test reliable. If you keep bubbling gas through for a long time the milkiness clears again, because excess carbon dioxide converts the carbonate into soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, the limewater test for carbon dioxide

explanation: A metal oxide is a base, so it neutralises an acid to give a salt and water — and nothing else. Black copper(II) oxide will not dissolve in water at all, but it dissolves readily in acid, and the colourless acid turns blue-green as copper(II) chloride forms. Notice there are no bubbles: that is the clearest way to tell a metal oxide from a carbonate, since a carbonate would fizz.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with metal oxides

explanation: Magnesium oxide is a basic oxide, so like copper(II) oxide it neutralises acid to a salt and water with no gas given off. The white powder simply disappears into the acid and the mixture warms up. Compare this with magnesium METAL in the same acid, which fizzes hydrogen off vigorously — the metal and its oxide behave quite differently, and telling them apart is a common examination question.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with metal oxides

explanation: Sulfuric acid is dibasic — each molecule gives away two H⁺ ions — so it takes two formula units of sodium hydroxide to neutralise one of acid, and the equation needs those coefficients to balance. Because twice as much water is being formed for each acid molecule, this releases noticeably more heat than the same amount of hydrochloric acid does. The salt left behind, sodium sulfate, is neutral, so the end point sits at pH 7.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, neutralisation and basicity of acids

explanation: Nitric acid is monobasic, like hydrochloric acid, so one formula unit of alkali neutralises one of acid and the heat given out is close to that of the hydrochloric acid reaction. This is because in every neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong alkali the same thing is really happening: H⁺ and OH⁻ joining to make water. The sodium and nitrate ions are spectators, and evaporating the solution would leave sodium nitrate crystals behind.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, neutralisation and preparation of salts

hazard.title: Flammable hydrogen gas is released
hazard.warning: The bubbles streaming off the zinc are hydrogen, which burns very easily and forms an explosive mixture with air.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Keep flames and hot surfaces well away while the metal is fizzing, and work in a well ventilated room so the hydrogen disperses.

explanation: Acid plus a metal above hydrogen in the reactivity series always gives a salt and hydrogen, whichever acid it is — only the salt changes. With hydrochloric acid zinc gives zinc chloride; with sulfuric acid the same metal gives zinc sulfate. This is the usual laboratory way of preparing hydrogen, and the gas is identified by the squeaky pop it makes with a lighted splint.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, reactions of acids with metals; Chemistry 9 — preparation of hydrogen

hazard.title: Choking ammonia gas is released
hazard.warning: Ammonia has a sharp, choking smell and irritates the eyes, nose and throat. Warming the mixture drives it off quickly, and leaning over the tube to smell it directly is genuinely harmful.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Work in a fume cupboard or a well ventilated room, and never inhale directly over the tube. To identify the gas, hold damp red litmus paper at the mouth of the tube rather than putting your nose near it.

explanation: This is the standard test for an ammonium salt. Any alkali will displace ammonia from an ammonium compound, but the mixture has to be warmed before enough gas comes off to detect — which is why nothing much happens in this vessel until the burner is turned on. Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas, so damp red litmus paper turning blue at the mouth of the tube identifies it beyond doubt.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — Acids, Bases and Salts, tests for ammonium salts

hazard.title: Soluble barium salts are poisonous
hazard.warning: The barium chloride solution used here is poisonous if swallowed. The barium sulfate it forms is harmless because it is so insoluble that the body cannot absorb it, but the solution it came from is not.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Handle barium solutions with care, wash your hands afterwards, and put the waste in the labelled heavy-metal container rather than down the sink.

explanation: This is the standard test for the sulfate ion. Barium sulfate is one of the most insoluble salts known, so the moment Ba²⁺ ions meet SO₄²⁻ ions a dense white precipitate appears. Sodium and chloride take no part and stay dissolved as spectator ions. In a real analysis the sample is acidified with hydrochloric acid first, so that a carbonate — which would also give a white precipitate — is destroyed before the barium chloride is added.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for anions, the barium chloride test for sulfate

explanation: Silver nitrate is the standard reagent for identifying halide ions, and it tells the three apart by colour: a chloride gives a white precipitate, a bromide a cream one, and an iodide this distinct yellow. All three silver halides are insoluble, so the precipitate appears at once. Potassium and nitrate are spectator ions. Doing all three side by side is the only reliable way to judge the colours, because cream and white are hard to tell apart on their own.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for anions, the silver nitrate test for halides

explanation: The middle member of the three halide tests. Silver bromide is cream — noticeably deeper than the white of silver chloride, but clearly paler than the yellow of silver iodide — and the colours deepen in that order going down Group 7. Silver bromide is extremely sensitive to light, and it was the compound coated onto photographic film for exactly that reason.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for anions, the silver nitrate test for halides

explanation: Adding sodium hydroxide to a solution of a metal salt is the standard way of identifying the metal ion, because most metal hydroxides are insoluble and each has its own colour. Copper(II) gives this pale blue jelly-like precipitate, and no other common ion looks like it. The clear blue solution turning into a blue solid that will not settle quickly is the giveaway. Warming the precipitate turns it black as it loses water and becomes copper(II) oxide.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for cations using sodium hydroxide

explanation: The test for the iron(II) ion. Sodium hydroxide precipitates a dull, dirty green solid quite unlike the clean colours of the other hydroxides. Left standing in air the surface slowly turns reddish brown, because oxygen converts iron(II) into iron(III) — which is the same change, and the same two colours, that you see when iron rusts.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for cations using sodium hydroxide

explanation: The test for the iron(III) ion, and the one that makes the pair of iron tests worth doing together: iron(II) gives a dirty green precipitate and iron(III) this unmistakable reddish brown. Notice the equation needs three hydroxides rather than two, because the iron here carries a 3+ charge instead of 2+. What forms is essentially rust.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for cations using sodium hydroxide

explanation: Magnesium gives a plain white precipitate with sodium hydroxide. Because several ions give white precipitates, a white result narrows the answer down rather than settling it — which is a useful lesson about qualitative analysis: one test rarely proves an identity on its own. The solid here is the same magnesium hydroxide sold as milk of magnesia for neutralising stomach acid.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — tests for cations using sodium hydroxide

explanation: A clean demonstration of a solubility rule: all sodium salts are soluble and all carbonates are insoluble EXCEPT those of Group 1 — so mixing a soluble calcium salt with a soluble carbonate must leave calcium carbonate behind as a solid. This is the same reaction that furs up kettles and pipes in hard-water areas, and the same white solid that makes limewater go milky.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — solubility rules and double displacement reactions

hazard.title: Lead compounds are poisonous
hazard.warning: Both the lead(II) nitrate solution and the white lead(II) chloride formed are poisonous. Lead builds up in the body rather than being cleared out, so even small repeated exposures matter.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Handle lead solutions with gloves and wash your hands afterwards. Collect all lead waste in the labelled heavy-metal container rather than washing it down the sink.

explanation: The solubility rule for chlorides is that they are all soluble EXCEPT silver, lead and mercury(I) — and this is that exception in action. Lead(II) chloride is unusual among precipitates because it is only slightly insoluble: warming the tube dissolves it again, and on cooling it comes back as glittering white needles. That reversibility is a good reminder that solubility depends on temperature.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — solubility rules for chlorides and their exceptions

explanation: No observable change. Work out what could possibly form: copper(II) chloride and sodium sulfate. Check both against the solubility rules — all common chlorides except silver, lead and mercury(I) are soluble, and all sodium salts are soluble — so neither product can leave the solution, and nothing precipitates. The blue simply stays blue. This is the routine you should follow before every double displacement: name the two possible products, look both up, and only expect a precipitate if one of them is insoluble.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 10 — applying solubility rules to predict double displacement reactions

hazard.title: Burning magnesium gives off blinding ultraviolet light
hazard.warning: Magnesium burns with an intensely bright white flame that contains a lot of ultraviolet. Looking straight at it can damage the eyes, and the flame is hot enough to set light to anything nearby. Water must never be used on a magnesium fire — it makes it worse, because magnesium reacts with steam.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Look at the flame indirectly or through darkened glass, never straight at it. Burn only a short piece held in tongs over a heatproof mat, and smother a magnesium fire with dry sand rather than water.

explanation: Oxidation in its oldest and simplest sense: a substance gaining oxygen. Each magnesium atom loses two electrons to an oxygen atom, so magnesium is oxidised and oxygen is reduced — the two always happen together, which is why these are called redox reactions. The white ash left behind is magnesium oxide, and it weighs MORE than the magnesium you started with, because the oxygen has been added to it.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, oxidation and reduction; Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactions of metals with oxygen

explanation: Copper is unreactive enough that it will not touch oxygen at room temperature — this is why copper roofs and pipes last so long. Heat it strongly, though, and the surface turns from reddish brown to black as copper(II) oxide forms. The colour change is easy to reverse: passing hydrogen over the hot black oxide turns it back to bright copper, which is the standard demonstration of reduction.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, oxidation as gain of oxygen

hazard.title: Hydrogen and a hot tube together
hazard.warning: Hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air, and this reaction needs the tube to be hot. Air left in the apparatus when the hydrogen is lit is what makes this dangerous rather than the reaction itself.
hazard.whatToDoInstead: Let the hydrogen flow long enough to sweep all the air out of the apparatus before heating, and keep heating until the flow is stopped so no air is drawn back in.

explanation: The mirror image of the reaction above, and the classic demonstration of reduction: the black copper(II) oxide LOSES its oxygen and turns back into bright reddish-brown copper, while the hydrogen GAINS that oxygen and leaves as water. Both halves happen at once — copper oxide is reduced, hydrogen is oxidised. Here hydrogen is acting as the reducing agent, which is exactly the job carbon monoxide does in a blast furnace when iron is extracted from its ore.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, reduction as loss of oxygen and the action of reducing agents

explanation: Halogen displacement is redox seen through electrons rather than oxygen. Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it takes the electrons: each chlorine atom gains an electron to become a chloride ion (chlorine is reduced), while each bromide ion loses one to become bromine (the bromide is oxidised). You can follow it by colour alone — a nearly colourless mixture turns orange-brown as bromine appears.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactivity of the halogens; Electrochemistry, redox as electron transfer

explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine as well, so it displaces it just as it displaced bromine — and the colour change is even more striking, from almost colourless to a deep brown as iodine forms. Because chlorine displaces both of the others, and neither of them can displace chlorine, chlorine must be the most reactive of the three.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactivity of the halogens

explanation: The middle step that settles the order. Bromine cannot displace chlorine, but it CAN displace iodine — the orange-brown of bromine deepens to the brown of iodine. Put together with the two chlorine reactions, this fixes the Group 7 order beyond doubt: chlorine, then bromine, then iodine, with reactivity falling as you go down the group.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, reactivity of the halogens

explanation: No observable change. Iodine is BELOW bromine in Group 7, so it is the less reactive of the two and cannot take the electrons away from bromide ions. The brown of the iodine simply stays as it was. This negative result is what makes the other three trustworthy: displacement works in one direction only, and finding the direction that fails is how the order of reactivity is proved rather than assumed.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Chemical Reactivity, establishing the order of halogen reactivity

explanation: Rusting is the slow oxidation of iron, and it needs BOTH oxygen and water — leave either one out and it does not happen, which is what the two entries alongside this one show. The iron loses electrons to oxygen, so the iron is oxidised. What makes rust so destructive compared with the oxide layer on aluminium is that it flakes off instead of sealing the surface, so fresh iron keeps being exposed. Painting, greasing, galvanising and sacrificial protection all work by keeping oxygen and water away from the metal, or by giving them something more reactive to attack instead.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, corrosion of iron and methods of its prevention

explanation: No observable change. Iron sitting in dry oxygen does not rust, however long it is left. This is one half of the classic three-tube experiment: iron in air and water rusts, iron in dry air does not, and iron in water with the air boiled out does not either. Both must be present together. It is also why tools kept in a dry store stay bright while the same tools left outside go orange within days.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, conditions necessary for rusting

explanation: No observable change. Iron under water that has had the air boiled out of it does not rust, because although water is present there is no oxygen for the iron to lose its electrons to. This is the other half of the three-tube experiment, and the pair of negative results together prove something a single positive result never could: that rusting needs oxygen AND water, not just one or the other.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry 9 — Electrochemistry, conditions necessary for rusting
